habitat: Long-eared bats are found across Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, including the British Isles across continental Europe to Japan. They inhabit deciduous and mixed forests, parklands, gardens, and agricultural areas with mature trees. During summer, they roost in tree cavities, attics, bat boxes, and occasionally caves. In winter, they hibernate in cool, stable environments such as caves, mines, cellars, and hollow trees. They are strongly associated with woodland edges and hedgerows where insect prey is abundant.
diet: Long-eared bats are insectivorous specialists, feeding primarily on moths — their favorite prey — along with earwigs, flies, beetles, and spiders. They employ a unique hunting strategy called 'gleaning': using their exceptionally sensitive hearing to locate prey by sound alone (passive listening), they pluck insects directly from leaves and bark while hovering. Their echolocation calls are extremely quiet ('whispering bats'), making them nearly undetectable to moths and other insects. They consume 20-30% of their body weight nightly.
behavior: Long-eared bats are gentle, slow-flying bats that emerge after full darkness. They are highly maneuverable, capable of hovering and flying through dense foliage with precision. Males are solitary during summer; females form small maternity colonies of 10-50. Their enormous ears — nearly as long as their body — are folded back or tucked under their wings during hibernation to prevent water loss. During hunting, the ears are held erect and rotated independently to pinpoint prey sounds with extraordinary accuracy. Courtship involves complex singing displays by males in autumn.
facts: Long-eared bats have ears up to 40 mm long — nearly as long as their entire body (45-55 mm). They can hear the footsteps of a moth walking on a leaf from several meters away. Their echolocation is so quiet (27-35 dB) that they are known as 'whispering bats' — essentially inaudible to bat detectors. They are highly susceptible to light pollution and habitat fragmentation. Their wing shape — short and broad — enables slow, maneuverable flight ideal for gleaning but limits their migration range. They can live up to 30 years, exceptionally long for a small mammal.
naming: Long-eared bat names might reflect their distinctive ears or whispering nature. Consider names like Radar, Whisper, Echo, Sonar, Batty, Dumbo, Biggs, Fennec (another large-eared mammal), Audie (for audio), Signal, or Doppler.
